At least 3 perfusion assessments: color + capillary refill + pinprick bleeding points (subdermal bleeding).

Priority in differential diagnosis: worsening pain with breast tension must first urgently rule out hematoma, and emphasize a low threshold for emergent return to the operating room for exploration.
Document ≥1 method to confirm exclusion of hematoma: bedside ultrasound / change in drain output volume and color / incision exploration (return to OR).

question: surgery_planning_002
rubrics: Frozen section/urgent pathology shows a “malignant small round cell/pleomorphic cell tumor”; epithelial markers do not support typical breast carcinoma.
Immunohistochemistry suggests skeletal muscle differentiation → intraoperative diagnosis favors primary breast soft-tissue sarcoma/rhabdomyosarcoma.

Must explicitly choose 1 of 2 intraoperative pathways: end the operation and stage first + MDT, then perform definitive surgery as a second-stage procedure vs immediate wider excision/mastectomy under strict criteria.
If choosing “stop and stage,” the rationale must state: sarcoma aims for planned R0 en bloc resection; avoid rushed extension that may cause contamination/unclear margins.

If intraoperative escalation to wider excision/mastectomy is chosen, the triggering criteria must be stated: uncontrolled bleeding requiring en bloc resection for hemostasis and other rare exceptions.
Exceptional indications for escalation also include: skin/chest wall invasion with impending ulceration/perforation, or obvious residual tumor that cannot be safely left in situ.
Intraoperatively, contamination must be explicitly avoided: prohibit repeated clamping, piecemeal additional excision, and cavity-wall curettage to pursue breast-cancer–style margins.
Emphasize the principle of local control: pursue planned negative margins/R0, en bloc tumor resection, and avoid rupture/dissemination.
An axillary strategy must be stated: SLNB/ALND is not performed routinely, because soft-tissue sarcoma predominantly metastasizes hematogenously and lymph node metastasis is uncommon.
State exceptions for axillary management: selective sampling only when axillary nodes are suspicious/positive or when sampling is needed to clarify staging.
Specimens must be oriented in a standardized manner: use sutures/clips to mark orientation, clearly document all margin information, and communicate/record this with pathology.

In the context of “rapid recurrence within a short time + suspicious ultrasound BI-RADS,” indicate this is more consistent with primary breast rhabdomyosarcoma/soft-tissue sarcoma rather than typical invasive carcinoma/inflammatory recurrence.
Emphasize that sampling must provide sufficient tissue for IHC ± molecular subtyping; avoid relying only on FNA or scant tissue that can cause misdiagnosis.
Preferred approach is image-guided core needle biopsy, with multiple cores obtained to meet IHC and, when necessary, molecular testing requirements.
State that the biopsy tract (needle or open/incisional) must be preplanned to allow subsequent en bloc resection and to reduce contamination/tumor seeding risk.
After diagnosis, immediately enter the sarcoma pathway for systematic staging; obtain at minimum a chest CT to assess for lung metastases (the most common site of distant spread).
Additional staging studies should follow MDT recommendations and may include PET/CT, abdominopelvic imaging, skeletal/bone assessment, and local MRI.
Local control should follow soft-tissue sarcoma principles: wide en bloc excision with a wide margin; avoid intralesional excision/piecemeal resection.
Clarify that the breast cancer SSO/ASTRO “no ink on tumor” margin standard does not apply to sarcoma; breast cancer guidelines cannot be applied to this case.
Axillary evaluation: perform axillary ultrasound first; if suspicious nodes are seen, confirm with image-guided FNA or core-needle sampling.
Explain that SLNB or axillary dissection is not performed routinely unless imaging/sampling confirms nodal involvement or there is a clear indication.

question: surgery_planning_003
rubrics: State that this is a reoperation: the ascending aorta cannot be safely dissected free/cannot be safely cross-clamped.
Identify the source of catastrophic risk: avoid any needle puncture or cannulation of the ascending aorta (e.g., root cardioplegia cannula, venting needle, etc.).

Make a choice based on the current situation: peripheral CPB has been established and the heart is still beating; continue management under these conditions.

Maintain effective left-heart decompression: ensure adequate venous return; if needed optimize gravity drainage or use VAVD.

Immediate bedside neurologic assessment: pupils + NIHSS/abbreviated exam; perform seizure monitoring/EEG as indicated.

Optimize ventilation and acid–base status: target PaCO2 per institutional strategy; avoid significant hypoventilation or excessive fluctuations.

Prevention: continuous CO2 insufflation (may specify 5 L/min) to reduce nitrogen fraction and promote gas dissolution and elimination.

question: surgery_planning_004
rubrics: Intraoperatively identify destructive prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) with aortic root/periannular abscess (periannular extension).
Clearly state the findings: near-circumferential dehiscence/complete detachment of the aortic valve prosthesis; annulus/proximal tissues “cannot hold sutures/no reliable annulus.”
Explain the causal chain: due to prosthesis detachment + root abscess + tissue unable to hold sutures, abandon conventional redo AVR and escalate to root reconstruction/total aortic root replacement.
The operative strategy must explicitly document “full root replacement/total aortic root replacement” or “conduit root reconstruction to the LVOT.”
After establishing stable CPB and myocardial protection, explant/remove the completely detached aortic valve prosthesis and address the associated structures.

Radical debridement must be “thorough to healthy bleeding margins,” and the periannular abscess cavity must be opened/irrigated to achieve source control.
Describe how a reliable proximal fixation/suturing platform is created during root reconstruction (e.g., reconstruct to the LVOT/healthy tissue).
Primary coronary reconstruction plan: mobilize the coronary ostia as coronary buttons and perform coronary reimplantation/ostial reconstruction.

Integrate the case anatomy: reoperation + complete prosthesis dehiscence (complete dehiscence) + ~80% perivalvular leak/defect → friable tissue that is difficult to suture.
Early ICU recognition should not rely on a single chest-tube output threshold; use a “constellation of signs” to judge surgical bleeding/anastomotic problems and differentiate tamponade phenotypes.
Chest-drainage example: >200 mL/h for several hours or a sudden large increase, with hemodynamic instability, should strongly raise suspicion for anastomotic bleeding.
Imaging stepwise pathway: bedside TTE/TEE to assess pericardial blood/effusion, perivalvular leak, and root status; if needed, CTA to localize pseudoaneurysm/leak.
In the ICU, resuscitate in steps first: rewarm to normothermia, replace calcium, correct acidosis, and control MAP/afterload to reduce anastomotic stress while preserving organ perfusion.
TEG/ROTEM or other viscoelastic testing must be used to distinguish coagulopathy vs surgical bleeding and to guide transfusion and coagulation-factor correction.
If bleeding or instability persists after TEG/ROTEM-guided correction → make a clear decision: return to the operating room for re-exploration/hemostasis is mandatory.
Re-exploration strategy: systematically inspect the root suture line/annular reconstruction and related suture lines, and the coronary ostia; prepare for CPB support.
If root rupture/pseudoaneurysm/severe paravalvular leak → definitive repair required, often redo root replacement.

Key prevention points: perform thorough debridement; all sutures must be placed in viable tissue. If the annulus/root cannot be reliably sutured, prioritize homograft or bioprosthetic root replacement.

question: surgery_planning_005
rubrics: State that this EUA is for redo/after failed repair or delayed reconstruction: the perineal body is completely absent/unidentifiable.
Identify anterior anal sphincter complex disruption/absence, with rectum and vagina apposed as a common wall/common plane (high-risk occult rectovaginal fistula).
Decision framework must assess contamination/infection: stool, purulence, vaginitis, or local infection, to decide same-setting reconstruction vs staged management.
Decision framework must assess tissue quality: scarring, dusky tissue without bleeding, inability to hold sutures, etc., prompting staging/diversion.
Enter through relatively normal/healthy tissue (can be lateral/proximal) and, under direct visualization, perform sharp dissection to develop the rectovaginal space.
The rectum and vagina must be repaired in separate layers independently; avoid “shared-wall” closure that leads to recurrent fistula.
After completing the repair, confirm integrity: rectal/vaginal leak testing (air test/water test, etc.).
Objectively identify sphincter ends: use a nerve/muscle stimulator to distinguish muscle from scar; confirm viable muscle by visible contraction.
Sphincteroplasty requires adequate mobilization to achieve a tension-free repair; overlapping repair is preferred, with end-to-end anastomosis as an alternative.

If a safe dissection plane cannot be established, there are repeated button-hole perforations, or the stump ends cannot be identified / a tension-free reconstruction cannot be achieved, convert to protective fecal diversion / staged repair.

Link fecal contamination/leakage/incontinence at 3 months with EUA findings of complete perineal body disruption plus absence/discontinuity of the anterior sphincter complex.

State clearly that this case is more consistent with persistent rectovaginal fecal contamination / an occult rectovaginal fistula rather than isolated sphincter failure: the shared rectal–vaginal wall/common plane was not separated.

Explain the mechanism: contaminated fourth-degree perineal tear + full-thickness vaginal laceration + sphincter disruption, without diversion → ongoing fecal contamination → infectious maceration → suture breakdown/dehiscence.

Diagnostic criteria: use EUA to assess defects of the rectal wall/posterior vaginal wall/shared wall, identify an epithelialized fistula opening or granulation/induration, and document vaginal fecal soiling/air bubbles.
In addition to EUA, add at least 1 objective test to confirm fistula/contamination (e.g., dye test, contrast study, or pelvic floor MRI/ultrasound).
In this case with recurrence, distorted anatomy, a shared wall/suspected rectovaginal fistula, and high contamination risk, strongly recommend fecal diversion: loop ileostomy or loop colostomy.
Reconstruction principles: perform layered, separated repair of rectum and vagina, reconstruct the perineal body and repair the sphincter complex, with staged surgery if necessary.
For recurrence or poor local tissue conditions, an interposition vascularized flap may be added: Martius flap (bulbocavernosus fat pad) or gracilis muscle flap.
Key postoperative protection points: during the stoma period, reduce fecal contamination and local tension; consider stoma reversal only after wound healing and absence of fecal vaginal soiling.

Preventive strategy—review the initial EUA: contamination + suspected rectovaginal communication + full-thickness vaginal laceration + poor bowel-control in children/easy loss to follow-up → consider fecal diversion earlier and more aggressively.

question: surgery_planning_006
rubrics: Clearly diagnose as complex multi-branch anal fistula: internal openings ≥2 (at 2 o’clock and 7 o’clock) with multiple branching tracts.
State that the 7 o’clock internal opening is suspected to be high: above the dentate line and close to the rectal mucosal side/rectal wall; management should be cautious.
The decision framework must center on “source control of infection + sphincter preservation,” prioritizing sphincter-sparing approaches.
If external sphincter involvement is significant/crossing proportion approximately >30% or in high, complex cases, avoid one-stage fistulotomy.
For the main tract crossing the external sphincter, use a loose draining seton: loose draining seton (silk/vessel loop), loose without constriction.
For a suspected high 7 o’clock internal opening/posterior intersphincteric tract: avoid blindly extending the incision upward through the sphincter or rectal wall to chase the internal opening.

The suspected confluence point/main drainage opening region requires prioritized, thorough drainage and assessment of tract communication to avoid missed cavities/spaces.

Early recognition of incontinence: be highly alert to leakage of flatus/liquid stool/formed stool, urgency, or decreased continence/control.
Recognition of persistence/recurrence: ongoing purulent drainage and a long-standing nonhealing external opening/incision suggest nonclosure or reinfection.

Mechanism must be linked to an anatomic threshold: for high/complex transsphincteric fistulae where the main tract traverses >30% of the external sphincter, fistulotomy is prone to cause incontinence.
Key recurrence anatomy must be explicitly named: presence of “two true internal openings” = an internal opening at the dentate line level + a high rectal mucosal internal opening.
Primary causes of recurrence/persistence must be stated: missing any true internal opening, or multiple secondary branches/undrained residual abscess cavities.
Staged treatment pathway: prioritize infection control/continued drainage first for source control (incision and drainage + retain/replace a loose seton traversing the main tract).
During the source-control phase, emphasize ensuring patency of drainage for all secondary branches and avoiding premature transection of the main tract drainage.
After inflammation resolves, proceed to sphincter-preserving closure: treat and close both internal openings separately to reduce recurrence and incontinence.

Follow-up investigations should be problem-triggered: endoscopic examination to assess internal opening/mucosal healing; if recurrence is suspected or an abscess cavity is not drained → MRI or transanal ultrasound.
Closed-loop prevention: preoperative MRI ± 3D reconstruction plus EUA under anesthesia to map two true internal openings, the course of the main tract, and multiple secondary branches.

question: surgery_planning_007
rubrics: Intraoperatively confirm that this case is a direct communication between a sacrococcygeal pilonidal sinus tract and an anal fistula internal opening at the 6 o’clock dentate line of the anal canal.

Clearly document the decision framework: control sepsis/source via drainage first → protect the sphincter → reduce wound burden and recurrence.
Anal fistula-side management: confirm the 6 o’clock internal opening by anoscopy/direct visualization; avoid enlarging the internal opening and avoid forceful probing.
Anal fistula-side source control: use sphincter-preserving drainage; a loose seton is one of the preferred options.
Priority transection point for “disconnecting the tract”: manage it at the perianal side close to the internal opening, rather than blindly transecting at the distal sacrococcygeal end.

Sacrococcygeal-side management: for the main cavity of recurrent pilonidal sinus, perform debridement and curettage of granulation tissue + removal of hair/foreign bodies + irrigation + ensure adequate drainage.
Must address the primary opening and the secondary sinus opening 3 cm away; clearly define their communication with the main cavity/branches and establish drainage.
Decouple the sacrococcygeal side from the perianal side: at this stage, prioritize adequate drainage; do not perform extended incision that creates a large wound surface.

Attribute the primary cause to ongoing contamination from an occult anorectal fistula, rather than simple pilonidal sinus recurrence/flap failure.
Must explicitly state the internal opening location: 6 o’clock at the dentate line level (near the dentate line).
Cite MRI evidence: confirm the presence of a sacrococcygeal pilonidal sinus/sinus tract and its association with an anorectal source.
Propose ≥3 warning triggers, including: persistent non-healing or purulent drainage for ≥2 months postoperatively.
Raise a red-flag trigger: recurrent suppuration/relapse despite prior flap or closure surgery.
Raise a red-flag trigger: probing/drainage suggests a deep tract course or recurrent abscess cavity formation.
Provide the staging strategy framework: first control infection and isolate contamination, then perform definitive reconstructive repair.
State the purpose of EUA (examination under anesthesia): identify the internal opening, define tract course, assess sphincter involvement, and evaluate for occult abscess cavities.
Stage 1 specific measures: adequate incision and drainage plus placement of a loose draining seton (loose seton) for infection control.
Explain why primary fistulotomy is not appropriate: suspected complex/high fistula or significant sphincter risk → avoid incontinence and a large wound.

question: surgery_planning_008
rubrics: Intraoperative frozen section/rapid pathology plus gross assessment: chronic excoriation-related changes (lichenification/lichen simplex chronicus spectrum), with no evidence of infection or tumor.
Redefine the problem as persistent dysesthesia in the postauricular graft/scar area: burning/electric-shock quality consistent with neuropathic pruritus.

question: surgery_planning_009

Convert to staged/delayed reconstruction if any of the following: no frozen section and margins uncertain, or the upper eyelid requires complex full-thickness reconstruction.

question: surgery_planning_010
rubrics: In this case, persistent hypotension on POD0–1 after pheochromocytoma resection should be attributed to suspected adrenal crisis/acute adrenal insufficiency.

question: surgery_planning_011

State the threshold to escalate/convert to open surgery: inability to clearly visualize the confluence, inability to apply a clamp at a right angle, inadequate countertraction, or any bleeding adjacent to the IVC warrants escalation.
Sudden hypotension ± tachycardia within 2 hours postoperatively: prioritize postoperative active bleeding/hemorrhagic shock.

question: surgery_planning_012
rubrics: Characterize the key problem as post-sleeve gastrectomy (SG) exaggerated enteroendocrine/satiety hormone effects causing “functional oral intake intolerance/anorexia and nausea,” rather than a structural complication.
Hormonal evidence must be cited: in a 3-hour standard meal test, fasting PYY is significantly elevated and rises further postprandially.
Hormonal evidence must be cited: active GLP-1 shows an early postprandial peak (approximately 15 minutes).
Explain that priority should be given to a “reversible, verifiable, titratable” mechanistic medication trial rather than proceeding directly to irreversible surgical revision.
First-line targeted strategy is a somatostatin analog (SSA) trial; e.g., short-acting octreotide (lanreotide acceptable).
Specify administration timing: use short-acting SSA before each meal/feeding to suppress PYY/GLP-1–related signaling/secretion.
Provide a reasonable starting dose and frequency range for short-acting octreotide: 25–100 μg per dose, as needed multiple times per day, with titration permitted.
Propose a pathway of “short-acting trial → objective verification → maintenance if benefit,” starting with a short-acting agent to enable rapid, reversible assessment.
Specify the assessment window: determine benefit within 3–7 days after initiation, or within several days based on objective endpoints.
List at least 3 case-relevant endpoints: nausea VAS, tolerable oral intake/feeding volume, degree of nasogastric-tube dependence/energy target attainment rate, weight trend/functional status.
Define failure/withdrawal criteria and an escalation plan: discontinue if no improvement after an adequate trial; switch to supportive nutrition and discuss subsequent options via MDT.
Frame this case as an “exclusion diagnosis”: exclude structural/mechanical/motility causes first, then consider functional intolerance.
State that stenosis, volvulus, ulcer, severe reflux, and other anatomic/structural problems must be excluded; explain “obstruction-like symptoms with negative investigations.”
Include exclusion of mimickers: mention that neuroendocrine tumor (NET) must be excluded before shifting to physiologic/hormone-driven mechanisms.

Objective confirmation: standardized meal challenge/mixed-meal test (after fasting, with a fixed and tolerated load) plus serial blood sampling to measure PYY/active GLP-1.
Blood sampling time points must cover 0–180 min and include an early 15–30 min point, with concurrent symptom quantification to establish hormone–symptom correlation.
Core management strategy: prioritize nutritional rescue and correction of electrolytes/micronutrients, then proceed to a monitorable targeted physiologic therapeutic trial.

The nutritional support pathway must be explicit: prioritize enteral feeding via NG/NJ (or a long-term plan); escalate to parenteral nutrition when necessary, for patients unable to maintain intake/progressive weight loss.

question: surgery_planning_013
rubrics: Intraoperative characterization as chronic mechanical obstruction: fixed incisura angularis stenosis plus sleeve-gastrectomy rotation/torsion, not edema/spasm.
Gastrotomy demonstrates large-volume food retention/phyto-bezoar, serving as evidence of fixed stenosis with stasis.
Propose intraluminal assessment and clearance of retained contents via gastrotomy, using at least two methods: suction plus grasping/basket/snare/irrigation.
During clearance, emphasize contamination prevention and avoidance of residual debris: minimize distal migration of fragments; use a specimen bag for extraction/incision protection when necessary.
Provide a decision pathway: BMI≈25, EWL≈98% but chronic obstruction + stasis → reconstruction is required for durable relief of obstruction.
Explain comparatively that endoscopic dilation alone has a high recurrence rate in fixed stenosis with torsion/long-segment disease and is not definitive.
Definitive option selection: convert to RYGB/Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (or equivalent bypass reconstruction) to relieve obstruction.
RYGB pouch-creation principle: create a “small but functional” proximal gastric pouch away from the incisura scar with good perfusion.
RYGB anastomosis principles: tension-free with good perfusion to prevent anastomotic stricture; appropriate limb length and routing.
Close mesenteric defects to prevent internal hernia; indications to convert to open surgery or modify the plan: heavy contamination, fragile/ischemic tissue, poor exposure, or bleeding.
Correctly identify the complication as an anastomotic or proximal sleeve staple-line dehiscence (leak) after revision/reconstruction.

Fully describe the pathophysiologic sequence: incisura stenosis/outflow obstruction → gastric content stasis → increased intragastric pressure/local ischemia → leak at the reconstructed site/staple line.
Explain high risk in this case based on the context: prior recurrent vomiting + gastric content stasis + incisura stenosis/outflow obstruction.
≥4 early warning signs, including tachycardia; and include either fever or one sign of sepsis.
First-line imaging pathway must include contrast-enhanced CT (oral ± IV contrast) to localize the leak and abscess.
State the treatment mainstay clearly: source control of infection + reduction of intraluminal pressure/relief of outflow obstruction + nutritional support.

Hemodynamically stable with localized fluid collection/abscess: broad-spectrum antibiotics + NPO + decompression (nasogastric tube/endoscopic decompression, etc.) + image-guided (percutaneous) drainage.
Hemodynamically unstable/diffuse peritonitis or failure of control: rapidly escalate to surgical exploration/source control and intensify resuscitation.
Emphasize that downstream stricture/outlet obstruction (incisura stricture) must be addressed to reduce intraluminal pressure and promote healing.
Endoscopic intervention as an option for persistent leak/inadequate drainage/bridge to surgery: name at least 2, e.g., covered stent, OTSC/clip, E-VAC (endoscopic negative-pressure therapy).

Prevention relevant to this case: preoperative nutritional assessment and correction of vitamin/trace-element deficiencies; control vomiting and feeding intolerance; endoscopic/imaging evaluation for stricture/torsion and hiatal hernia/GERD.

question: surgery_planning_014
rubrics: Intraoperatively must clarify: laparoscopy showed no adnexal/broad ligament mass; the lesion was located on the right anterior abdominal wall peritoneal covering.
Must describe localization details: approximately 3 cm from the right edge of the prior transverse incision; solitary ~4.5×4.0 cm pink-white, smooth, well-demarcated mass.
A systematic abdominal exploration should be performed to exclude other primary lesions or peritoneal dissemination/implantation.
Decision-making must compare “en bloc” resection versus oncologic biopsy (excisional/incisional/wedge).
State the purpose and triggers for frozen section: send for frozen section when the nature is uncertain or when immediate decisions are needed regarding margins/extent of invasion.
Tumor-free technique: avoid grasping or compressing the tumor itself; perform sharp and blunt dissection along planes in surrounding normal tissue.
If necessary, resect en bloc with the overlying peritoneum to reduce rupture and seeding risk and to ensure adequate margins.
The specimen must be placed into an endobag and removed through an extended port site/small incision.
Must state explicitly: morcellation is strictly prohibited; avoid tumor rupture as much as possible.
Assess tissue planes before resection: whether extraperitoneal, whether involving rectus abdominis muscle/fascia/anterior sheath, vascular supply, and continuity with scar tissue.
If the fascia/anterior sheath is involved, layered, tension-free closure is required; for large defects, assess the need for mesh and/or reconstruction.

Must list indications for escalation/ conversion to open surgery/ consultation: unclear boundaries making margins difficult to ensure, extensive adhesions, large defect, uncontrolled bleeding, or rupture/forced entry.
Based on POD3 incisional erythema, swelling, warmth, pain + subcutaneous fluctuance + low-grade fever + ultrasound showing a pre-fascial hypoechoic fluid collection, propose the diagnosis.
The three-tier differential must include: seroma/hematoma vs superficial SSI/localized abscess vs necrotizing fasciitis (low probability, high risk).
Identify red-flag signs of deep fascial infection/necrotizing fasciitis: rapid progression, pain out of proportion, skin necrosis/crepitus, toxemia.
Mechanism: en bloc excision of a right anterior abdominal wall mass + separation of the peritoneum from abdominal wall layers → potential dead-space formation.
Additional mechanism: manipulation near a prior transverse-incision scar + highly vascular mass → oozing/lymphatic drainage impairment causing seroma/hematoma.
Propose route of secondary infection: fluid accumulation in dead space → bacterial proliferation → superficial SSI/localized abscess; severe cases may extend to deep fascia.
Prompt diagnostic workup should include vital signs + sepsis screening (qSOFA/sepsis risk assessment).
Mention at least 2 laboratory tests: CBC, CRP, procalcitonin; lactate may be added for perfusion/sepsis assessment.
If there is drainage or aspiration/drainage is planned: send specimens for bacterial culture + susceptibility testing; first-line imaging is abdominal wall ultrasound, with escalation as needed.
Management should prioritize source control: abscess/incisional infection requires same-day or ≤24–48 h needle aspiration or incision and drainage + debridement + culture.
Antibiotic strategy: seroma without infection does not require routine antibiotics; if infected, start empiric coverage for common skin flora and de-escalate/escalate based on culture results.
If necrotizing fasciitis is suspected: immediate surgical exploration and wide debridement; do not wait for culture or imaging results.

question: surgery_planning_015
rubrics: Identify high risk in this case: a giant prolapsed pedunculated submucosal leiomyoma causing severe distortion of the cervix/lower uterine segment, making anatomic planes difficult to delineate.
Clearly identify sources of urinary tract injury risk: possible medial displacement of the ureter/close proximity to the danger zone + shallowing of the vesicocervical space.
Recommend stopping first: pause blind clamping of the uterine vessels/energy transection/blind incision of the vaginal cuff; re-establish exposure first.
No-go zone principle: do not transect the uterine vessels or incise the vaginal cuff until the relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery/vaginal cuff incision line is clearly defined.

Provide a decision branch: if exposure is poor, consider transvaginal devascularization/pedicle control or excision of a pedunculated submucosal fibroid to correct distortion and improve the visual field.
Alternatively, perform retroperitoneal dissection first/convert to retroperitoneal dissection: establish a safe ureteral anatomic plane before addressing key vessels and the vaginal cuff.
Ureteral protection workflow: enter the retroperitoneum to identify the ureter → trace distally to the uterine artery crossing/ureteral tunnel/paracervical segment.
Complete ureterolysis and lateralization, and maintain continuous visualization during key steps such as uterine vessel transection and vaginal cuff incision.

Safe sequence: after adequate bladder dissection and downward mobilization, with the ureter lateralized/visible, manage the uterine vessels close to the uterine side first, then incise the vaginal cuff.

Name pitfalls and provide a contingency plan: blind clamping without seeing the ureter/thermal injury/advancing despite poor visualization → if hemostasis cannot be ensured under direct vision, promptly convert to laparotomy/change the approach.
Oncologic safety: inability to obtain endometrial tissue preoperatively and a potential lesion not excluded → remove the specimen as intact as possible and avoid morcellation.

Oliguria plus flank pain/fever 24–72 h postoperatively, or increased clear fluid from the vagina/drains, should raise strong suspicion for ureteral or bladder injury (urine leak/obstruction/extravasation/delayed presentation after thermal injury).

Given this case of a giant prolapsed submucosal fibroid causing severe distortion of the cervix/lower uterine segment, identify medial displacement of the ureter and its close proximity to the uterine artery crossing as a high-risk site for inadvertent ligation or thermal injury.
Identify the vaginal cuff colpotomy line and the paracervical vascular bundle/need for extensive paracervical dissection and ureterolysis as high-risk steps for urinary tract injury.
First diagnostic step: confirm Foley catheter patency and replace if needed; perform bedside bladder ultrasound scan to assess urinary retention and exclude non-injury causes.
If bladder injury is suspected: propose a bladder instillation test/dye test (e.g., instill and observe whether vaginal/drain output becomes dyed) for rapid bedside screening.
Stepwise imaging: prioritize CT urography (CTU) or intravenous pyelography to assess extravasation/obstruction and hydronephrosis.
If localization is required, propose endoscopy/contrast study: cystoscopy plus retrograde ureterography to define the site and severity of injury.
Small bladder laceration/micro-leak with stable vital signs: continuous bladder decompression with indwelling catheter for ~7–14 days ± anti-infective therapy, with follow-up to confirm closure.
Larger bladder laceration or a clearly identified intraoperative/early perforation: immediate layered suture repair with continuous bladder decompression via indwelling catheter.

Suspected ureteral contusion/partial obstruction/early thermal injury: urgent urology consultation; prioritize retrograde placement of a double-J ureteral stent for drainage, typically left in place for ~4–6 weeks.

Complete ureteral transection or inability to place a stent / infectious sepsis: consider percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) drainage; delay definitive repair with timing based on infection control and clinical opportunity.

Prevention: pre-/intraoperatively identify “giant prolapsed fibroid + loss of cervical/lower uterine segment anatomy” as high risk; expose the ureter first, then address the paracervical/vaginal fornix region; obtain early urology consultation if needed.

question: surgery_planning_016
rubrics: At 48 h exploration after Xiapex (collagenase) injection: the small finger FDS and FDP show acute/fresh-appearing complete transection (double rupture).
Specify that the rupture site is within the injection-related “thick cord/band” or “pathologic soft-tissue area,” and assess the usability of the inflammatory tendon bed.
State the criteria for primary in-situ repair: tendon ends can be approximated with low tension, without requiring extreme wrist flexion or finger flexion to achieve coaptation.
Primary repair must also meet: no obvious necrosis/nonviable tissue in the bed, and the pulley system/tendon sheath can largely be preserved or only minimally addressed.
Management of small-finger double tendon rupture: prioritize FDP repair to restore DIP function and overall flexion.
The FDS decision must be explicit: it may be left unrepaired or only one slip/bundle repaired, to reduce bulk and adhesions.
Repair the primary tendon (usually FDP) with a strong multi-strand core suture: locking/grasping configuration, ≥4 strands (prefer 4–6 strands or equivalent).
Add a circumferential epitendinous suture over the core repair; keep a low-profile construct and optimize knot placement to reduce friction and facilitate early protected mobilization.

Extend exposure and protect the digital nerves/digital arteries; excise/release only the Dupuytren cords that impede tendon gliding, avoiding excessive palmar fasciectomy that may devascularize the digit.
Pulley/tendon sheath strategy: if needed, perform a limited vent to allow smooth gliding, avoiding bowstringing and triggering.

Indications for staged reconstruction: still unable to achieve tension-free coaptation, tendon quality cannot hold sutures/repair is prone to gapping, or pulley/tendon sheath loss or collagenase injury predicts very poor gliding.

Document intact neurovascular status: preserved sensation and normal distal perfusion/capillary refill.

Confirmation strategy must include imaging: when rupture is suspected, use ultrasound or MRI to assess FDP/FDS continuity and the location of the tendon ends.
Management pathway: if onset ≤48 h and FDP+FDS rupture is suspected/confirmed, perform early/urgent surgical exploration to define the rupture plane and tendon quality.
Intraoperatively, choose primary repair or staged reconstruction based on tendon quality/tendon bed/pulley conditions, and address glide-limiting Dupuytren cords/pulleys.
Primary repair technique must specify a 4–6-strand core suture + circumferential epitendinous suture, following flexor tendon repair principles.
Postoperative rehabilitation must include a dorsal blocking splint + early controlled motion to prevent adhesions and rerupture.

Recurrence prevention: strictly perform intralesional cord injection; avoid excessive depth near the flexor tendon sheath/tendon; control dilution/dose/injection sites; for high-risk digits such as the small finger, consider ultrasound guidance.

question: surgery_planning_017
rubrics: Identify the situation as loss of the operative field/bleeding within a narrow transoral endoscopic working space, with fibrosis and high-risk limited superior-pole exposure.
When IONM shows traction-related signal deterioration, stop dissection and initiate a traction timeout; releasing/reducing traction is the first priority response.

Propose measures to improve superior pole exposure: adjust retraction, pull the gland downward, and manage superior pole vessels close to the gland, etc.

After crisis management, the goal remains completion of the originally planned right thyroid lobectomy (a change in approach does not mean extending the extent of resection).

Simultaneously and systematically rule out false signals: poor ETT electrode contact, lead connection/grounding problems, and anesthesia-related neuromuscular blockade/signal attenuation.

Intraoperative prevention key points: fully establish the skin flap and working space; early segmental control of superior pole vessels/veins; reduce sustained medial traction and instrument torque.

question: surgery_planning_018

Near the laryngeal entry point/Berry ligament, minimize use of energy devices close to the nerve to prevent thermal spread injury.

If sustained amplitude decline/suspected LOS occurs, first exclude artifact: endotracheal tube (ETT) electrode malposition/rotation, secretions, neuromuscular blockade anesthesia, and wiring/equipment issues.
If safe confirmation is not possible or adhesions are severe, perform a nerve-sparing shave leaving a thin tissue layer; if necessary, stop and treat in stages.

Explicitly identify the key risk in this case: threat to the “only functional cricoarytenoid joint/single available cricoarytenoid unit,” with minimal contralateral compensation.

question: surgery_planning_019
rubrics: Intraoperative scenario: during planned curative right hepatectomy/ablation, multiple enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the hepatoduodenal ligament, approximately 0.9 cm.
In the setting of HBV positivity plus suspected cirrhosis, state that the porta hepatis lymph node status can directly determine whether to proceed with right hepatectomy/ablation that day.

Reassess before irreversible steps: perform systematic exploration to exclude extrahepatic disease (including the lesser sac and other key abdominal regions) before deciding to proceed.
Use intraoperative ultrasound ± Doppler to re-confirm the three right-lobe lesions and their relationship to the portal vein/hepatic veins, to adjust the resection/ablation plan.

Frozen section positive: manage as biologically aggressive disease more consistent with ICC/mixed tumor, re-weigh benefit vs risk, and consider aborting a large-volume right hepatectomy and changing the plan.
Frozen section negative: more supportive of localized disease such as HCC; after confirming no other extrahepatic disease, proceed with the planned right hepatectomy/ablation.

Initial management emphasizes source control and supportive care: resuscitation, analgesia, nutritional support; empiric anti-infective therapy when necessary.
Use contrast-enhanced CT (± ultrasound) to assess intraperitoneal fluid collection, biloma/abscess, and to determine whether existing drains are patent.
If fluid collection is present or drainage is inadequate, perform image-guided percutaneous aspiration/catheter drainage as the preferred first escalation.
If the bile leak persists/is high-output or distal obstruction is suspected, escalate to ERCP: sphincterotomy ± biliary stent to reduce biliary pressure.
If ERCP fails or cannot be performed, perform PTBD; peritonitis/sepsis or failure of source control are indications for reoperation.

Prevention: perform preoperative MRCP or intraoperative biliary assessment to define anatomy/variants; avoid excessive skeletonization of the hepatic hilum causing bile duct ischemia; individually ligate/suture-ligate each visible bile duct on the transection surface.

question: surgery_planning_020
rubrics: Identify “coexisting two lesions”: a 2.2 cm solid mass at the right hepatic hilum + a multiloculated cystic lesion abutting/encasing the common hepatic duct.

Prevent two types of failure simultaneously: use early margin assessment plus mapping frozen section (FS) to reduce R1; use repeated reassessment to avoid over-resection/unreconstructable extended surgery.

question: surgery_planning_021
rubrics: Interpret a “stone fixed/suspended on the anterior bladder wall” as a foreign-body stone caused by erosion/migration of hernia repair mesh into the bladder.

Complication B recognition and prevention: an anastomosis that is too low or sphincter-complex injury → impaired continence (with anterior urethral/vaginal injury risk); keep the anastomotic line above the dentate line and protect the anterior plane.
Differentiate mechanical outlet obstruction (anastomotic stricture/residual aganglionic muscular cuff/posterior “shelf”) from Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC); they may coexist.
Systematic severity assessment must include: vital signs plus perfusion/urine output; labs including CBC ± differential, CRP, electrolytes/acid–base status.
If fever or signs of toxemia are present, blood cultures must be obtained and the patient managed according to septic-shock risk.
Imaging must first exclude perforation: obtain an abdominal plain radiograph to assess bowel dilatation, air–fluid levels, and free intraperitoneal air.

At the bedside, perform a gentle digital anorectal examination and/or attempt passage of a large-bore catheter to assess passability, presence of a constricting ring/stricture, fecal impaction, and ability to pass flatus/stool.

If needed, propose examination under anesthesia (EUA) with analgesia/anesthesia: directly inspect/palpate the anastomosis and assess for stricture, torsion/flap-valve obstruction, and residual muscular cuff/posterior wall remnant.
Contrast enema is a selective test: consider only after perforation is excluded, the child is stable, and adequate decompression has been achieved.

Must explain the mechanism in this case: an ultra-low anastomosis near the dentate line plus posterior longitudinal split incision increases risk to lumen caliber/blood supply, leading to a fixed stricture or a posterior-wall “shelf.”
In the acute phase, manage as Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) ± obstruction: nil per os + IV fluids with electrolyte correction; add nasogastric decompression if needed.

Must include rectal decompression (large-bore catheter) plus regular warm saline rectal irrigations to promote passage of flatus/stool, and state that antibiotics are initiated when HAEC or toxemia is suspected/confirmed.

Provide at least one escalation/de-escalation criterion: inability to pass catheter or a fixed stricture ring; persistent obstruction despite decompression/irrigation; recurrent/refractory HAEC; EUA demonstrating a posterior-wall “shelf” or residual muscular cuff → consider dilation and/or reoperation.

question: surgery_planning_032
rubrics: Can identify that after releasing the clamp the composite segment rapidly becomes dark and swollen (turgid), with brisk capillary refill and continuous distal oozing.
Explicitly attribute the above findings to impaired venous outflow (acute venous congestion), not inadequate arterial inflow.
Decision priority: when acute venous congestion occurs, immediately add/improve venous outflow as the top priority; emphasize that 2–3 venous outflow channels are often required.
Simultaneously confirm/complete ≥1 reliable arterial inflow anastomosis and ensure patency (may be managed in parallel; do not rigidly mandate sequence).
First rule out mechanical causes: K-wire traction, twisting of the composite segment, pedicle compression, retractor/dressing compression, and positioning-related venous kinking.
Describe establishing reliable outflow: select healthy recipient vessels; if necessary, perform additional venous anastomoses or venous grafting to increase multi-channel outflow.
Explicitly name ≥3 high-risk pitfalls for venous anastomotic failure: tension/kink/pedicle twist/compression/thrombosis.

If venous congestion persists or thrombosis recurs after additional venous anastomosis/venous grafting: proceed to early take-back for revision or redo of the anastomosis; change recipient vessels if necessary.
When perfusion is unstable, explicitly propose delaying tendon and nerve repair and final closure, prioritizing stabilization of inflow and outflow.
Escalation when unsalvageable: if stable outflow/inflow cannot be established, consider aborting or changing the reconstruction plan (e.g., leave temporarily unclosed / plan staged reconstruction).
Given “multi-digit composite replantation + arterial signals remain good,” clearly diagnose venous congestion/venous outflow obstruction (venous congestion).
Differentiate from arterial ischemia: arterial Doppler signal/bleeding still present; findings include cyanotic swelling and rapid capillary refill with dark blood.
Explain a mechanism consistent with a saw injury plus crush–avulsion and contamination: tissue fragmentation and edema in the injured zone cause impaired venous return.

State that composite multi-digit replantation has a high venous outflow requirement; an insufficient number/caliber of venous anastomoses (number of veins < number of arteries) is a correctable cause.
State that venous contusion/intimal injury can cause early thrombosis or anastomotic stenosis, especially in crush–avulsion zones.
State that the course at the wrist/anatomical snuffbox is prone to kinking; external fixation or overly tight sutures/excessive skin tension can compress veins.
Immediate bedside management: loosen dressings/splint/overly tight sutures; position the wrist in neutral to avoid pedicle twisting/kinking; elevate and keep warm to correct hypothermia.
Concurrently optimize hemodynamics at the bedside: maintain normal blood pressure and avoid excessive vasoconstrictors that impair replant perfusion.

Immediately reassess perfusion: arterial Doppler signal, fingertip color/temperature, capillary refill, and the character of bleeding; if no improvement, escalate to urgent return to the operating room.
Reoperation should focus on restoring/increasing venous outflow: explore and correct anastomotic kinking/tension, evacuate hematoma, and relieve compression.

Add/replace with larger, healthier venous targets: choose dorsal veins or larger systemic veins away from the crush zone; perform vein grafting if needed, with attention to valve direction and verification of patency.

question: surgery_planning_033
rubrics: At 6 hours postoperatively, marked scalp swelling plus large-volume subcutaneous drainage/oozing, in the setting of 35 h warm ischemia, suggests a threatened replantation.
Even if the anastomotic Doppler has a signal and pinprick bleeding is present, microcirculatory perfusion failure/reperfusion injury cannot be excluded.
Given rapidly progressive swelling/exudation plus high risk from 35 h warm ischemia, maintain a low threshold for prompt return to the OR for urgent re-exploration rather than observation.
First priority on return to the OR: repeat objective perfusion assessment (ICGA or an equivalent method), with focused reassessment of previously low-perfusion areas.
Decompression is mandatory on return to the OR: open/loosen part of the sutures to relieve tension and compressive effects in the subgaleal space.
Evacuate and adequately drain subgaleal hematoma/seroma; address the collection causing large-volume subcutaneous exudate.
Systematically evaluate and correct inflow/outflow problems: pedicle kinking/compression, tunnel or dressing compression, and other mechanical factors.
If needed, explore/correct anastomotic problems and inadequate venous return, and implement measures to increase inflow/improve venous drainage.

If, after decompression and confirmation of vascular patency, extensive persistent hypoperfusion or ongoing clinical deterioration remains, transition to an early staged debridement plus reconstruction plan.
For marginally suspicious/low-perfusion areas, mark or zone-document and reassess dynamically; avoid immediate one-stage wide excision.

With obvious scalp swelling at 24–48 h post-op and high-volume subcutaneous drainage, but persistent Doppler signal and pinprick bleeding, the leading diagnosis is inadequate venous drainage/venous congestion.
Explicitly state that ischemia–reperfusion injury is related to the 35 h warm ischemia in this case.
Mechanism must include: endothelial dysfunction → microcirculatory no-reflow/microthrombosis → worsening venous congestion.
Mechanism must include: increased capillary permeability (capillary leak) causing abnormal edema and increased drainage output.
Propose early postoperative repeat ICGA/indocyanine green angiography, with comparison to the intraoperative baseline, as an objective reassessment.
Clearly state that ICGA relative perfused area <25% indicates a warning of “occult perfusion failure,” and based on this intensify re-evaluation/intervention.
Recheck hemoglobin and coagulation studies within 24–48 h to differentiate blood loss/oozing from congestive exudation and to guide management.
If necessary, perform bedside ultrasound to assess subgaleal fluid collection/hematoma as an etiologic evaluation for swelling and abnormal drainage.
State urgent re-exploration/return to OR, with the indication being progressive deterioration (increasing swelling/decreased perfusion/worsening drainage).

Prevention points must target near-total scalp replantation with 35 h warm ischemia: minimize ischemia time as much as possible + preoperatively correct anemia/coagulopathy + intraoperatively prioritize establishing sufficient venous outflow (multiple venous anastomoses/venous grafting if necessary).

question: surgery_planning_034
rubrics: Classify “extensive intramural mucoid esophageal wall lesion + luminal stenosis + longitudinal extent exceeding preoperative assessment + atypical planes” as potential malignancy/intramural spread.
Manage as potentially mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma; immediately pause irreversible steps: do not construct the gastric conduit or perform anastomotic site selection/positioning.
Crisis communication: promptly inform the team of abnormal intraoperative extent; adjust the goal to maximize R0 resection and avoid blind reconstruction.
On-site re-verification of involved extent: palpation + intraoperative esophagoscopy as needed / re-check preoperative localization to confirm proximal and distal resectability.
Specify the need for frozen section / intraoperative rapid pathology; submit both the proximal and distal resection margins.
In addition to both margins, obtain representative samples from the most suspicious intramural mucinous lesion area and send for frozen section.
Orient and label the margins/specimen (proximal/distal, etc.) and document to ensure pathology can interpret margin status.
Establish a closed loop: positive or highly suspicious margin → extend resection → repeat frozen section → continue until margins are negative (end point).

If iterations remain positive / multifocal skip involvement is suspected / frozen section is indeterminate but gross appearance suggests extensive malignancy → abort or stage the procedure, avoiding forced reconstruction.
Proceed to irreversible reconstruction steps (gastric conduit construction/route/anastomosis) only after pathology is clearly defined and both proximal and distal margins are negative.
Mucin/tumor contamination control: avoid creating the gastric conduit/anastomosis first to prevent contamination; isolate the specimen and change instruments and gloves to reduce dissemination risk.
On postoperative day 5, fever/chest pain/dyspnea with a sudden increase in pleural drainage that is milky-white; initial diagnosis: chylothorax/thoracic duct injury.
Confirm by at least 1 criterion: pleural fluid triglycerides >110 mg/dL or >1.24 mmol/L; or presence of chylomicrons/positive fat stain.
In the differential, consider empyema: turbid purulent pleural fluid with positive culture and/or elevated neutrophils, to distinguish from chylothorax.
While confirming chylothorax, concurrently exclude anastomotic leak/mediastinal infection: chest CT ± oral water-soluble contrast.
Mechanism: traction/thermal injury during two-field lymph node dissection, or incomplete ligation/clipping causing injury to the thoracic duct or variant branches.
Name at least 1 high-risk area: lower mediastinum/subcarinal region/left lower mediastinum/paraaortic region/near the azygos arch.
Immediate management includes: ensure patency of closed chest drainage + respiratory and circulatory support + infection assessment; correct nutritional/electrolyte disturbances.
Conservative treatment includes at least 2 of the following: NPO or low-fat + MCT diet, TPN, octreotide; and reduce chyle production.
Use drainage volume/trend to set escalation: persistent high output (e.g., >1 L/day) or no decrease over several days → early thoracic duct ligation or endovascular embolization.

Prevention key points: during mediastinal dissection, proactively identify the thoracic duct course and variants (anterior to the vertebral body/paraaortic/near the azygos vein/supradiaphragmatic); avoid blind dissection with energy devices.

question: surgery_planning_035
rubrics: Clearly identify the key intraoperative warning signs: multiple hard, anthracotic, structurally irregular ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes.
State that at least 1 suspicious lymph node is densely adherent to the pulmonary artery (PA) adventitia, indicating increased risk of bleeding/vascular injury.
Based on “accurate staging + local control + operative safety,” escalate the strategy from limited node sampling to systematic MLND/MLNS.
Systematic assessment must cover both hilar (N1) and mediastinal (N2) stations, and be verifiable by anatomic location rather than simply “taking a few nodes.”
Explain that in the setting of Cushing syndrome/ACTH secretion, complete tumor resection and reliable staging are even more necessary to guide subsequent therapy.
Propose sending frozen section only when it would change the intraoperative strategy, rather than routinely adding operative time.
Timing for frozen section: as early as possible before further irreversible steps; prioritize the PA-adherent N1 node or the most suspicious mediastinal node.
Specify how frozen section may alter the course: if N2 or multistation metastasis is confirmed, consider aborting curative resection and transitioning to other treatment plans.
For VATS management of a PA-adherent node: obtain stable exposure/adjust traction and port placement first, then dissect to avoid traction on the PA.
Communicate with anesthesia to control blood pressure/reduce PA tension, and prepare vascular clamps and sutures to manage PA injury.

Define escalation/conversion criteria: if exposure is inadequate or the risk of bleeding from dissection adjacent to the pulmonary artery (PA) increases, convert to thoracotomy; avoid blind forceful dissection.
If suspicious ipsilateral hilar/mediastinal lymph node (LN) metastasis is seen intraoperatively, escalation from limited sampling/N1-only dissection to systematic LN assessment is mandatory.
State the rationale for escalation: to avoid missed N2 disease causing understaging and staging bias, which affects oncologic decision-making.
State the oncologic consequence: N1-only/limited sampling may leave regional micrometastatic disease, increasing the risk of ipsilateral hilar recurrence.
Incorporate case characteristics: ACTH-secreting bronchopulmonary carcinoid/neuroendocrine tumor is not a low-risk entity in which LN evaluation can be omitted.
Cite the cohort evidence from the stem: LN metastasis in this population is not uncommon, approximately on the order of “one third,” supporting systematic assessment.
The intraoperative plan must specify: systematic mediastinal LN dissection or systematic station-based sampling, covering both N1 (hilar/interlobar) + N2 (mediastinal).
Key mediastinal stations must include subcarinal station 7 (other N2 stations may also be listed to ensure coverage).
Specify quantitative thresholds and documentation: harvest/dissect by station and submit specimens labeled by station; ensure complete intraoperative and postoperative pathology documentation.
Perform frozen-section pathology for suspicious or key-station LNs; use frozen-section results as an intraoperative decision trigger.
If frozen section suggests N2 positive: first assess whether R0 resection can still be achieved without incurring disproportionate risk.
If N2 positive and R0 remains achievable: favor completing the planned anatomic resection plus systematic lymph node dissection to obtain complete staging.

Perioperative closed-loop plan: preoperative MDT to preset “upgrade to combined N1+N2 assessment whenever suspicious lymph nodes are seen”; intraoperatively avoid N1-only evaluation; postoperatively recheck ACTH as early as possible to assess Cushing’s remission.

question: surgery_planning_036
rubrics: Intraoperatively identify an intraluminal polymer ligating clip in the left ureter as an iatrogenic foreign body from prior surgery, with clip impaction/partial encrustation.
Describe clip-associated mucosal hyperemia and fragility causing adjacent stricture; proximal turbid urine/pyuria indicates infectious obstruction.

Establish the causal chain: infectious obstruction + inability to reliably pass a guidewire/inability to establish a safety wire → prioritize immediate source control with drainage and decompression during the same session.
Use “whether a safety guidewire/access can be established under direct vision with low risk” as the key threshold for deciding whether to continue endoscopic manipulation.
Explicitly prohibit repeated blind guidewire probing; avoid submucosal tunneling/false passage that can cause injury or perforation.
Use low-pressure irrigation and minimize renal pelvic pressure to reduce the risk of infection spread/bacteremia.
Obtain proximal turbid urine/pyuria for culture (± susceptibility testing) as the basis for infection management and subsequent antibiotic selection.
Only attempt limited crossing under direct vision using a hydrophilic guidewire ± an angled/torqueable catheter; stop immediately and withdraw if resistance is encountered.

List ≥2 triggers to abort/escalate: inability to quickly and safely establish access; clip clearly fixed/impacted; extravasation/suspected perforation; bleeding causing loss of visualization; significant infection burden with concern for bacteremia.

If safe crossing is not possible, complete definitive management during the same session: stop retrograde maneuvers and perform percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) drainage for decompression (direct PCN acceptable).
Consider endoscopic clip removal only after a safe guidewire/access tract has been established and the visual field/working space is controllable, and only if the clip is not deeply fixed.
Principles of clip extraction: remove encrustation first to relieve impaction; use minimal traction and avoid axial force; keep energy application away from the ureteral wall.
After removal of an impacted/encrusted polymer ligation clip (mid-to-distal ureter), remain alert for ureteral perforation/avulsion → urinary extravasation/urinoma → infection.

Mechanism must be stated: long-term clip impaction with chronic inflammatory encapsulation causes stricture; a safe guidewire is difficult to pass, and traction/thermal cutting/sounding can cause full-thickness tear.
Explain that turbid proximal urine suggests infection with obstruction; manage according to the infection + obstruction pathway before any endoscopic manipulation.
Provide ≥3 triggers raising suspicion: worsening pain; fever/tachycardia; increased WBC/CRP; decreased urine output/poor drainage on the affected side; worsening hematuria; persistent pyuria.
Preferred imaging must be specified: CT urography/delayed-phase CT to assess urinary extravasation, urinoma, and degree of obstruction.
Clearly state the “infection + obstruction” priority principle: perform upper urinary tract decompression/drainage + antimicrobial therapy + source control first, then address the clip/stricture.
Stable small leak/contained urinoma: retrograde placement of a JJ stent for internal drainage + antibiotics; may add Foley catheterization to reduce reflux.
Failed retrograde stenting or persistent leak/sepsis: percutaneous nephrostomy for decompression ± percutaneous aspiration/drainage of urinoma/abscess.
Major injury/suspected avulsion (mid-to-distal ureter): choose surgical repair matched to injury location, e.g., ureteroneocystostomy ± psoas hitch/Boari flap.

Intraoperative prevention must fit this case: do not force advancement without a safety wire; if the working space is small with fixed inflammatory edema, decompress first or stage the procedure before definitive management.

question: surgery_planning_037
rubrics: Clearly describe the intraoperative findings: longitudinal arteriotomy of the left CCA revealed dark-red organized/chronic thrombus; proximal suction produced no back-bleeding.
Determine this as chronic/organized CCA occlusion with thrombus extending proximally toward the subclavian origin (low-lying, outside the operative field).
Based on “dark-red organized thrombus + no back-bleeding on suction + extension to the subclavian,” judge high embolic risk and avoid blind instrument probing.
Prioritize cerebral perfusion in decision-making: use NIRS and/or SSEP to assess clamp tolerance; any signal drop triggers restoration of perfusion.
Perform distal protection before proximal instrumentation: at minimum clamp the ICA; if needed, clamp the ECA/ICA branches to prevent debris from entering the intracranial circulation.
Initiate systemic anticoagulation: IV heparin, with concurrent heparinized saline irrigation (heparinized saline irrigation).
Specify the need to determine the proximal extent of the occlusion and whether “true proximal control” can be obtained (cervical segment vs supraclavicular/thoracic inlet).
Propose a feasible proximal recanalization option A: extend supraclavicular/thoracic inlet exposure to obtain true proximal control and manage/remove thrombus.
Propose a feasible proximal recanalization option B: hybrid approach with sheath placement via the incision/direct puncture and fluoroscopy-guided recanalization.
Completion assessment: controlled back-bleeding/antegrade inflow testing, with intraoperative imaging to confirm recanalization and patency.

Indications to escalate/convert: worsening NIRS/SSEP, anticipated prolonged clamping, inability to safely achieve proximal control, or absent pulsatile inflow after thrombectomy → switch to a rapid reperfusion strategy.
New focal neurologic deficit within 6 hours postoperatively: first consider ipsilateral ischemic stroke/carotid endarterectomy–related ischemic event.
Mechanism must be integrated with this case: proximal left CCA occlusion below the clavicle not directly visualizable + unstable bifurcation plaque + poor collateral circulation.
Must consider thromboemboli arising from unstable plaque and/or instrumentation.
Must consider early thrombotic occlusion or hypoperfusion causing inadequate flow to the reconstructed segment/intracranial circulation.
Emergency management sequence: first perform bedside ABC assessment and inspect the neck incision to rule out a tension hematoma/progressive swelling causing airway compression.
At the bedside, simultaneously correct hypoxemia and hypotension; individualize MAP augmentation to optimize cerebral perfusion before proceeding to imaging.
Imaging pathway must include: immediate non-contrast head CT to exclude hemorrhage.
Imaging must include: head and neck CTA to assess patency of the reconstructed left CCA/ICA/ECA segment and evaluate for intracranial large-vessel occlusion.
If needed, add bedside carotid ultrasound and/or CTP to assess perfusion.

Triage based on imaging: acute occlusion/thrombus of the reconstructed segment → emergent reoperation; intracranial large-vessel occlusion → thrombectomy; note that IV thrombolysis is usually contraindicated postoperatively.

Intraoperative prevention addressing “proximal subclavian segment not directly visible + unstable plaque”: avoid blind proximal recanalization or repeated instrument passage through the occluded segment.

Prevention must propose reliable proximal control: extend the incision supraclavicularly for exposure; if necessary perform partial sternotomy/alternative inflow, and coordinate with flushing and monitoring-triggered actions.

question: surgery_planning_038
rubrics: Before clamping during exposure, TCD shows left MCA mean flow velocity 70→13 cm/s (decrease >80%), interpreted as abrupt ipsilateral cerebral perfusion drop/compromised ICA inflow.
Identify discordant monitoring: even if NIRS shows only mild change or does not reach threshold, a >80% abrupt drop on TCD remains a highly dangerous signal.
Rapidly exclude artifact: verify TCD probe position/insonation angle and MCA signal quality; also confirm NIRS sensor placement.
Recheck systemic reversible factors without delaying: confirm MAP, PaCO2/EtCO2, and oxygenation are stable or correctable.
If MAP/EtCO2 are stable and this is an ipsilateral event, prioritize management as a carotid inflow problem rather than continued observation.
Immediate intervention: stop dissection immediately; release traction/retractors; avoid compressing the carotid sinus or ICA.
Coordinate with anesthesia to raise blood pressure: increase MAP by 20–30% above baseline, and maintain normocapnia to mild hypercapnia with adequate oxygenation.
If low flow persists (>1–3 minutes or recurrent and difficult to correct), gently obtain controlled proximal and distal vascular control of the CCA/ECA/ICA.
With ongoing hypoperfusion, perform rapid shunting after heparinization and/or proceed immediately to arteriotomy to identify the cause (test clamp not mandatory).

If TCD remains severely low after pressor support plus shunting/repair, or if new EEG abnormalities occur/shunt flow is inadequate, perform intraoperative ultrasound or angiography to assess for distal ICA dissection, etc.
Before clamping, left MCA TCD mean velocity 70→13 cm/s (>80% decrease) is judged a critical warning sign of acute ipsilateral cerebral perfusion compromise.
Do not dismiss the ischemic threat because NIRS decreases only 7% and EEG is unchanged; prioritize management as a true event.
Explain discordant monitoring: an abrupt TCD drop suggests a sudden reduction in left ICA inflow; NIRS/EEG may lag or be insensitive.
Before clamping, prioritize reversible mechanical causes: retractor/vascular loop compression or kinking, or traction from neck positioning.
Immediately pause dissection/current maneuver; first relieve mechanical factors: loosen or remove retractors and vascular loops, and reposition the neck to avoid traction.
Rule out artifact first: check TCD probe position and signal quality; if needed, reposition/re-secure to confirm the reading is real.
Optimize cerebral perfusion in parallel: increase MAP; correct hypocapnia and hypoxemia; if needed, give fluids/vasopressors to improve CBF.
If TCD does not recover, initiate intraoperative duplex/intraoperative ultrasound or handheld Doppler to localize ICA/carotid stenosis, dissection, or thrombus.
After localization, propose a corrective pathway: surgical correction (relieve kinking, patch/repair) or thrombectomy; if needed, consider shunting/aborting the procedure.
Prevention: set trigger thresholds and a team script—if there is a sustained/significant TCD decrease, activate the algorithm: rule out artifact first, then relieve mechanical factors.
Prevention: gentle dissection; minimize ICA traction and retractor pressure; avoid overly tight or prolonged vascular-loop compression.
